userPrompt: Can I require employees to work more than 48 hours a week in the EU?
responseText:
**No, in general you cannot lawfully require employees to work more than 48 hours per week (including overtime) in the EU.**

### Key Legal Rule
The **EU Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC)**, transposed into national law in all 27 Member States, sets a **maximum average of 48 hours per week** over a reference period (usually 4 months, sometimes longer). This limit is mandatory and applies to almost all workers.

### What “48 hours” includes
- All hours worked for the employer
- Overtime
- On-call time that counts as working time (varies by country and ECJ case law)

### Important exceptions and nuances
- **Opt-out**: Many countries (UK before Brexit, Germany, France, etc.) allow **individual opt-outs** where the employee voluntarily agrees in writing to work more than 48 hours. The opt-out must be freely given, can usually be withdrawn with notice, and the employer must keep records.
- **Certain sectors/professions** have special rules or longer reference periods (e.g. healthcare, transport, seasonal work).
- **Collective agreements** or national law can set stricter limits or different averaging rules.
- Some countries impose lower caps (e.g. France’s 35-hour legal week + overtime rules, or stricter daily/weekly limits).

### Practical answer for an employer
- You **may not impose** a requirement to work >48 hours on average as a condition of employment in most situations.
- You **can** ask employees to sign an opt-out agreement where permitted.
- Even with an opt-out, you must respect daily rest (11 consecutive hours per 24h), weekly rest, and maximum daily working time (usually 10–13 hours depending on the country).
- You must maintain **objective, reliable records** of actual hours worked (ECJ ruling C-55/18 *CCOO*).

### Recommendation
Check the **specific national law** of the Member State(s) where the employees work. Rules on opt-outs, reference periods, on-call time, and enforcement differ significantly (e.g. stricter in France, Belgium, Netherlands; more flexible in Germany or the UK pre-Brexit model).
